metadata.title: Development of the reading literacy questionnaire for EFL learners at primary schools

survey_design.weight_fields_interpretation: The study collected self-report questionnaire data from 784 Grade 3–6 primary students in China across six schools in six provinces, using classroom administration and anonymous/voluntary participation. The analysis was conducted with SPSS 26.0 and Amos 23.0, focusing on content validity, item analysis, exploratory factor analysis, confirmatory factor analysis, reliability (Cronbach’s alpha), and criterion validity (Pearson correlation). The manuscript does not report the use of complex survey sampling weights (e.g., student design weights) or any replicate-weight scheme, and the methods are psychometric validation rather than population-representative estimation. Therefore, no explicit weight variable is applied or discussed; results should be interpreted as validity/reliability evidence for the developed instrument within this sampled context rather than as nationally representative estimates.

data.handling_not_reported_explanation: This study develops and validates a self-report reading literacy questionnaire using Likert-scale items and psychometric analyses (EFA/CFA, Cronbach’s alpha, Pearson correlations). Plausible Values (PV) are not applicable because the dependent variables are questionnaire responses and scale scores rather than ILSA cognitive achievement scales that use PVs. Missing-data handling is not reported because the paper does not describe any imputation or deletion rule for incomplete questionnaires/scales; it only reports effective response rates for the two stages.

sample_details.sample_filtering_criteria: Two-stage design. Stage 1 (Feb 2022): 420 valid questionnaires were obtained from 450 distributed (effective response rate 93.3%). The 21-item initial questionnaire was split by grade into Sample Group A (N=210) for predictive validation (content analysis, item analysis, EFA) and Sample Group B (N=210) for construct validation (CFA). Items were later revised after EFA: Q1, Q10, Q11 deleted for low factor load (<0.5); Q9, Q14, Q15, Q17 deleted for inconsistent content; dimensions were condensed into three factors with 14 remaining items. Stage 2 (Mar 2022): the revised 14-item questionnaire was administered to the same six schools; 364 valid questionnaires and 364 valid criterion scales were obtained (effective response rate 91%). Criterion validation and reliability were computed using the 364 participants who completed both the ERLQ and the Chinese Students’ English Rating Scale.

main_findings.standardized_conclusion: Using PISA the study leveraged the reported predictors to predict Reading Literacy, finding that This paper is not an ILSA/PISA-style predictive ML study; it develops and validates a self-report English Reading Literacy Questionnaire (ERLQ) for EFL learners in primary schools. Using a two-stage sample of Chinese Grade 3–6 students (Stage 1: N=420 split into two groups of 210 for EFA and CFA; Stage 2: N=364 for criterion validation), the authors used psychometric validation procedures rather than machine learning prediction. For the initial 21-item version, item analysis showed significant item discrimination (item-total correlations r=0.591 to 0.852, p<0.01), and EFA led to a revised 14-item, three-dimension structure with cumulative explained variance of 59.876%. For the revised instrument, CFA fit indices were acceptable (CMIN/DF=1.508, GFI=0.935, AGFI=0.907, NFI=0.909, IFI=0.968, RMSEA=0.049), reliability was high (Cronbach’s alpha=0.904), and criterion validity was strong (Pearson r=0.871, p<0.01). Limitations include a relatively small, localized sample and no reported missing-data handling or survey-weighting strategy. This indicates that these patterns have implications for educational policy and instructional practice, though cross-sectional ILSA designs cannot establish causality.

data.null_fields_interpretation: The extraction is sparse for ML-specific fields because the manuscript is an instrument development/psychometric validation study (content validity, EFA/CFA, reliability, criterion validity) and does not train or evaluate any machine learning predictive models. Consequently, there are no ML target variables, no PV-based achievement outcomes, and no ML performance metrics to populate.
